references.text: Earlier in the same chapter, the principle of double restitution for theft is established, which is also applied here in verse 6.
Describes the situation where the thief is not found and the case must be brought before God—a continuation of the laws regarding entrusted property.
Addresses similar situations where someone has received goods from their neighbor to keep, including cases of theft and fraud.
Laws concerning restitution and guilt when one has acted treacherously against a neighbor, relevant to the principle of entrusted property.
Proverbs warns against putting up security for another person's debt, touching on the theme of responsibility for others' property.
The parable of the talents deals with entrusted goods and the responsibility to manage what has been placed in one's care.
Jesus teaches about faithfulness in managing what has been entrusted to us, including other people's property.
A thematic parallel showing the development from the concrete penal law (double) to the wisdom literature's principle that theft leads to total ruin (sevenfold).
Direct contextual connection within the same legal code comparing responsibility for theft of entrusted property versus damage to borrowed items.
Leviticus 5:23 confirms and expands the principle in Exodus 22:6 by including 'entrusted property' as a category requiring full restitution before atonement.
